## Understanding the MICS6 numeracy assessment {#c02-numeracy}

The MICS6 foundational numeracy assessment consists of 21 items organised into four tasks.

Unlike reading, the numeracy assessment does not involve language-specific passages of different lengths. This makes the data simpler to prepare for multi-country analysis, although researchers should still examine country questionnaires and routing.

UNICEF describes the four domains as number reading, number discrimination, addition, and pattern recognition.

### Structure of the assessment

| Task | Number of items | What the child does |
|---|---:|---|
| Number reading | 6 | Reads numbers shown by the interviewer |
| Number discrimination | 5 | Identifies the larger of two numbers |
| Addition | 5 | Solves addition problems |
| Pattern recognition and completion | 5 | Identifies the missing number in a sequence |
| Total | 21 | |

The standard MICS6 booklet moves from relatively simple items to more demanding ones within the assessment.

### 1. Number reading

The child is shown six numbers and asked to identify each one.

The standard assessment includes numbers ranging from one to three digits.

The official MICS task indicator requires the child to answer all six items correctly.

### 2. Number discrimination

The child is shown five pairs of numbers and asked to identify which number in each pair is larger.

The official task indicator requires all five items correct.

### 3. Addition

The child is given five addition problems.

These include simple single-digit calculations and more demanding items.

Successful completion of the MICS addition task requires all five items correct.

### 4. Pattern recognition and completion

The child is shown five number sequences with a missing value and asked to supply the missing number.

The official task indicator requires all five items correct.

### Foundational numeracy requires mastery of all four tasks

The official MICS6 definition is deliberately stringent:

```text
6/6 number-reading items
          AND
5/5 number-discrimination items
          AND
5/5 addition items
          AND
5/5 pattern items
          │
          ▼
FOUNDATIONAL NUMERACY SKILLS
```

UNICEF's standard tabulation plan specifies that a child must correctly complete every item within each task and all four tasks to demonstrate foundational numeracy skills.

See the [UNICEF FLS module adaptation guidelines](https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/FL-module-adaptation-guidelines-August-21-2019.pdf).

### The binary indicator hides a lot of information

Because the official measure requires success on every task, children with very different skill profiles can receive the same value.

```text
                    Number   Discrim.   Addition   Pattern    Total
Child A               6/6      5/5        5/5       4/5      20/21
Child B               3/6      1/5        0/5       0/5       4/21

Foundational
numeracy?              NO       —          —         —          NO
```

Both are classified as not demonstrating foundational numeracy skills, but their observed performance is clearly very different.

For research purposes, it is often informative to examine each of the four task indicators, the individual items, number of items correct within each task, total items correct out of 21, and the overall foundational-numeracy indicator.

Which measure is appropriate depends on the research question.

### Stop rules and non-attempts

The standard questionnaire includes interviewer instructions and stop rules within parts of the numeracy assessment. Item responses can therefore distinguish correct, incorrect and no-attempt outcomes.

When constructing scores, do not automatically treat every blank or non-attempt as equivalent without checking the questionnaire routing.

The worked examples later in this guide show how AFLEARN constructs transparent numeracy scores from the item-level data.

### Comparing numeracy across countries

Numeracy avoids some of the language-specific complications of reading, but comparison still requires care.

In particular, consider age, grade, whether the child is currently attending school, exposure to schooling within the current year, survey timing, and differences in schooling systems.

A Grade 3 child assessed near the beginning of a school year has had less exposure to Grade 3 instruction than a Grade 3 child assessed near the end of the year. This matters when interpreting apparent cross-country differences.

### Headline indicators and distributions answer different questions

The MICS foundational-numeracy indicator answers:

> What proportion of children demonstrate mastery of all four specified foundational numeracy tasks?

A total score answers a different question:

> How many of the 21 observed numeracy items can children answer correctly?

Neither is universally preferable. Choose the measure that matches the research question and describe it accurately.

The worked examples in [Worked examples](#c06-worked-examples) use both approaches.
